AZ-2026-SB1560.aiSummary: Arizona raised the maximum loan from the water supply development revolving fund for water supply projects from $3 million to $20 million. The fund can also still be used for grants, technical help, debt purchases or refinancing, bond insurance help, running the fund, and water supply studies. The bill was signed into law on June 22, 2026.

AZ-2026-SB1497.aiSummary: This law changes rules for school district self-insurance programs, which are district plans that pay some losses themselves instead of buying full insurance. It lets districts form or join pooled programs, sets rules for trust funds, audits, and liability coverage, and requires some districts to get price quotes every three years. It also requires detailed cost, claim, drug, and enrollment data from the people who support these plans.

AZ-2026-SB1336.aiSummary: This law changes how the state land department handles state trust land, including rules for public records, appraisals, maps, and lease or permit timing. It also sets new duties for the department to make and update military-related maps and share them with the public, counties, cities, and the state real estate department. AZ-2026-SB1189.aiSummary: The law changes rules for revitalization districts, which are public groups that handle local projects and services. It lets them make more contracts, set user fees, borrow money, and work with towns, tribes, and others on infrastructure, but it bars them from using district money for pro sports stadiums or team-only facilities. It also requires new construction contracts to include rules that let contractors and subcontractors stop work if they are not paid, and it applies to contracts signed after the law takes effect.

AZ-2026-HB2700.aiSummary: Arizona would create a temporary study committee on assistive technology. The group would meet twice a year, study new tools and ways to better serve people who use assistive technology, and submit a report by October 1, 2027. Some members could be paid back for travel and other allowed expenses, and the committee would end on that same date.

AZ-2026-HB2105.aiSummary: The measure would require the state tax department and county assessors to tell property owners before an on-site inspection and give the inspection date. They would also have to give the owner a copy of the inspection report, and the notice would not have to be sent by certified mail. For farm property, it keeps the yearly inspection and four-year appraisal rules, and blocks another on-site inspection for three years after the last one unless there is a change in use, a split, a change in ownership or lease, or a taxable improvement.

AZ-2026-SB1511.aiSummary: The bill would require a person with a nondomiciled commercial driver license to show lawful immigration status or lawful presence before driving a commercial motor vehicle in Arizona. If the driver cannot show proof, police could issue a citation, assess a civil penalty, and report the case to the licensing authority and federal trucking officials. It would also allow the driver to be placed out of service, require the motor carrier to get a replacement driver or move the truck within 24 hours, and could lead to impoundment of the truck and related cargo costs.

AZ-2026-HB2322.aiSummary: The bill would require the Department of Child Safety to record, by audio or video, interviews it conducts with children, unless equipment fails or is not available. It would also require the department to apply for federal grants for that recording work if such grants are created, and the law would take effect only if that federal grant law is enacted by December 31, 2036. AZ-2026-HB2140.aiSummary: The bill would let the state treasurer invest some trust and treasury money in physical gold or silver bullion, up to 10% of the total value, if it is kept in a U.S. precious metals depository that meets storage, insurance, audit, and separate-holding rules. It would also update other rules on how the treasurer can invest state money and lend securities. The measure passed the legislature but was vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-HB2133.aiSummary: The bill would require commercial websites that publish sexual material to verify that each depicted person gave written, verifiable consent and was at least 18 when the material was made. It would also require them to keep verification records for seven years and use reasonable steps to block uploads without verified consent. The bill would expand rules on unlawful disclosure of nude or sexual images to include synthetic depictions made with artificial intelligence or other technology, and it would let the state and the person shown bring civil cases.
